results.text: ENERGY COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 14 Oil Recent developments In mid-October, front-month Brent futures reached about $110 per barrel (bbl) as markets weighed rising crude supply and an accelerated release of emergency oil stockpiles by International Energy Agency (IEA) members against conflict in the Middle East (figure 7.A). Entering October, average Middle East oil exports approached their 2025 level owing to greater use of ship-to-ship transfers and untracked shipments (figure 7.B). The recovery was concentrated on crude oil and condensates, while oil products exports, including diesel, have lagged, partly because refinery damage. Tanker shortages, which drove Gulf voyage rates to record highs, together with intensifying attacks on vessels, thinning inventories and concerns about longer-term supply, kept Brent prices elevated (figure 7.C).

Monthly data from various editions of the IEA ’s Oil Market Report for global observed inventories. Last observation is September 2026. The gray area depicts the range of inventories for each month over 2021–25. C. Changes in U.S. exports and China’s imports in each month compared with values in February 2026. Values are in gross terms and include both crude oil and oil products. D. The implied oil market balance is the difference between supply and demand. Data based on IEA ’s Oil Market Report (October 2026 edition). Wholesale prices of key oil products, especially diesel and jet fuel, have climbed considerably more than those of crude oil since March (figure 2.A). This mainly reflects the effects of Middle East supply outages, as well as attacks on oil infrastructure in the Russian Federation, following its invasion of Ukraine.

events.query: global natural gas production forecast 2027 percent bcm

results.text: ENERGYCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 21 Global natural gas production is projected to decline by 0.8 percent (35 bcm) in 2026. A drop of more than 11 percent (90 bcm) in the Middle East—driven by damage to gas-processing and LNG facilities—is expected to be partly offset by increases of 3.2 percent (42 bcm) in North America and 2.1 percent (18 bcm) in Eurasia. Global production is forecast to increase by about 2.5 percent (110 bcm) in 2027, led by nearly a 5.5 percent (39 bcm) recovery in the Middle East, with the region’s output expected to remain below its 2025 level because of reduced LNG export capacity in Qatar and delays to its North Field expansion. Production is also expected to rise by 3 percent (41 bcm) in North America, 2 percent (15 bcm) in Asia Pacific, and 1 percent (10 bcm) in Eurasia.

In 2027, global consumption is forecast to grow by 2.6 percent (110 bcm), led by increases of about 7 percent (43 bcm) in the Middle East as industrial production and gas processing normalize, and 4 percent (about 40 bcm) in Asia Pacific.

In contrast, the U.S. benchmark is projected to remain unchanged in 2026 (y/y), and to increase by about 6 percent in 2027 and about 5 percent in 2028, mainly driven by growing external demand for LNG. Global natural gas consumption is projected to decline by about 1 percent (50 bcm) in 2026 (figure 10.D). Demand is expected to decrease by about 8 percent (50 bcm) in the Middle East, reflecting disrupted industrial demand. In Europe and Asia Pacific, consumption is set to soften by 2.5 percent (13 bcm) and about 1 percent (9 bcm), respectively, as power-sector use declines. By contrast, Eurasian demand is projected to rise as residential consumption rebounds after mild weather in 2025.

Among grains, price pressures are most pronounced for wheat, amid several headwinds to production and trade. Wheat prices are projected to jump by 28 percent in 2026 and 14 percent in 2027, before easing by 11 percent in 2028. Global wheat output is expected to contract by 3 percent in 2026–27 with reduced harvests in several major producing countries.

In sum, production declines and export disruptions are expected to reduce global wheat exports by 7 percent in 2026–27, with shipments falling across all nine leading exporters. answer: In the Special Focus of the report, the commodity groups identified as net transmitters of price volatility include industrial metals and food commodities. Conversely, livestock and soft commodities are noted as net receivers of volatility. Energy and precious metals are generally balanced between transmitting and receiving volatility, although their roles can vary in specific episodes, such as during COVID-19 when they became net transmitters while food commodities became net receivers [world-bank-cmo-2026-10:62:paragraph-900:3][world-bank-cmo-2026-10:59:paragraph-900:1].

The aggregate measures thus establish the extent of connectedness, but not which groups primarily transmit or absorb volatility or the different roles of commodities within a group. Transmitters and receivers Commodity groups can be similarly connected to the broader system while playing very different roles within it. Directional connectedness separates volatility transmitted to other groups from volatility received from them. The full-sample results show a clear hierarchy: industrial metals and food transmit more volatility than they receive; livestock and soft commodities receive more than they transmit; and energy and precious metals are broadly balanced between the two roles (figure SF .1.D). Net connectedness—the difference between transmitted and received connectedness—provides the clearest summary of this hierarchy.

results.text: Urea prices are forecast to fall by 16 percent in 2027 and 14 percent in 2028, assuming Middle Eastern exports recover, natural gas prices ease, Fertilizers The World Bank Group’s fertilizer price index fell by 22 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q) and continued to decline in October, fully reversing the 2026Q2 surge that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Urea prices drove both swings, while other fertilizer prices rose less sharply but remained elevated in 2026Q3. Despite the recent retreat, the index is projected to rise by about 14 percent in 2026 (y/y), reflecting shipping disruptions in the Middle East, associated increases in input costs, and trade restrictions. Prices are forecast to fall by 12 percent in 2027 and a further 8 percent in 2028 as input costs ease and supplies recover, aided by increased exports from producers outside the Gulf region.

Upside risks to the outlook for urea prices include an escalation in the Middle East conflict that raises input costs, particularly for natural gas, above baseline expectations. More specifically, continued conflict could lead to an extension of Qatar’s force majeure, imposed in March, on contracts to sell LNG and related products, including urea. Export restrictions by major producers are another potential source of renewed price surges. Conversely, a swift reduction of geopolitical tensions in the Gulf region could lead to a surge of exports, materially lowering prices, although infrastructure damage is likely to delay the full recovery of urea production. After a projected 7 percent increase in 2026, DAP prices are forecast to drop by about 18 percent in 2027 and 17 percent in 2028.

MOP has been largely shielded from the Middle East conflict, as production in the Gulf region is negligible, and as potash is mined rather than produced from natural gas. Supply has also been supported by the easing of U.S. sanctions on Belarus, the third-largest producer after Canada and Russia. As a result, MOP remains the most affordable fertilizer relative to food prices (figure 18.D). Outlook and risks Despite recent declines, urea prices are projected to average 21 percent higher in 2026 (y/y), reflecting the surge in the first half of the year. Seasonal buying from Brazil, which typically purchases most of its urea imports between August and December, is likely to support prices in late 2026.

results.text: Other critical minerals Prices of other critical minerals generally weakened in 2026Q3, led by cobalt, which fell by 25 percent (q/q), and lithium, which declined by 13 percent (figure 20.A). The decline in lithium prices reflected the restart of previously curtailed mines in Australia, the resumption of concentrate exports from Zimbabwe, and softer EV sales momentum in China, although strong demand from energy storage and robust EV demand in several other regions provided support. Cobalt prices fell sharply, partly reversing earlier gains, but remained elevated as export quotas in the Democratic Republic of Congo continued to constrain global supply. Rare earth prices were broadly stable, with ongoing Chinese export controls and licensing requirements curbing supply in some markets outside China.

Nickel demand from battery production, however, is being tempered by the growing use of nickel-free lithium-iron-phosphate batteries in EVs and energy storage. After a projected 13 percent increase in 2026 (y/y), nickel prices are forecast to be little changed in 2027 as market conditions rebalance, before firming by 1 percent in 2028. Tin prices rose by 4 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), reaching all-time highs amid persistent supply constraints, and remained broadly stable in October. Tin supply is expected to recover gradually as mine production continues to normalize in Myanmar following policy-related disruptions, and regulatory and export constraints ease in Indonesia. Rising tin output should ease the market tightness seen in 2026, although limited expansion among other producers and a thin pipeline of new mining projects are expected to constrain future supply growth.

These measures may gradually lead to more geographically diversified production, bolstering FIGURE 20 Critical minerals markets Critical mineral prices generally weakened in 2026Q3, with cobalt and lithium falling while rare earth prices were broadly stable. However, supply restrictions continued to support prices in some markets. New trade- policy interventions have remained common, with restrictive measures far outnumbering liberalizing actions in recent years. Export restrictions and strategic stockpiling could lift international prices in the near term, while efforts to expand mining, processing, and recycling capacity may gradually improve supply resilience. Yet with demand projected to rise sharply and new projects facing long lead times, critical mineral markets are expected to remain highly sensitive to policy changes and disruptions for some time. A.
